@@

+- Before summing items that the source presents under a caption, establish which rows belong to that caption. When a heading line (a category name ending in a colon, such as a securities/asset group) is followed by itemized lines and then by further lines at the parent level of the same list, include only the itemized lines the caption governs; exclude neighbouring parent-level lines even when the parsed text reproduces every line at identical indentation, since flattened extraction removes the visual nesting. If membership is ambiguous, resolve it with evidence available to you rather than by assuming the nearest lines belong: compare the itemized rows against a subtotal or grand total the table already reports, or consult another edition/table that displays the same grouping with clearer structure; when a table supplies an explicitly labelled total or subtotal row or column for the requested aggregate, read that labelled entry instead of assembling the aggregate yourself. Where the ambiguity cannot be resolved from the retrieved text, prefer the narrower membership (only the lines explicitly itemized under the caption), because adding parent-level lines inflates a subtotal.
 - When a monthly or other period statistic is computed from more than one supplied bulletin, first choose the table that actually contains every requested period and extract the full set from it. Then check the other supplied bulletins for overlapping periods; if a later bulletin shows a revised value for an overlapping period, use the later revised value for that period while retaining the complete table's values for periods it alone covers. Do not switch to a different fiscal-versus-calendar series merely because a later table exists. Reconcile the complete monthly set before computing the statistic.
editor.reason: Added a grouped-caption operand-selection rule in Evidence Discipline, with ambiguity resolution and a narrower-membership fallback, before the existing multi-bulletin computation guidance.

+++ b/SKILL.md
@@
 - Start by narrowing to the most likely candidate file before reading long passages.
+- Treat candidate file names in the question as names to locate, not as usable tool arguments. Resolve a file before searching inside it: call glob once with a simple pattern (the bare file name, or a single listing of available documents) and pass the exact path that glob returns, including any directory prefix, to every later grep or read. After a rejected-path observation, do not repeat grep/read against the same bare name and do not escalate to broad patterns that return no matches; if a name-based glob finds nothing, list the corpus once and continue with the returned path. This path resolution comes before the search-and-read steps, and the retrieved text, not the path, remains the evidence.
 - Prefer targeted search terms that name the exact entity, period, measure, or table concept from the question.
